newsitem.title: USA: Campbell Soup ends months of speculation, picks new chief.
newsitem.headline: Campbell Soup ends months of speculation, picks new chief.

text.p: Campbell Soup Co. Monday ended months of speculation by naming a successor to the dynamic David Johnson as president and chief executive and announcing Johnson would step down as chairman next year.

The company said Dale Morrison, 48, a former PepsiCo Inc. marketing wizard who helped drive strong sales gains in Campbell-owned brands such as Pepperidge Farm Goldfish crackers, would take over as president and chief executive officer beginning July 15.
Johnson, 64, is to remain chairman until July 31, 1998, Campbell said. That is one year beyond the expiration of his current five-year contract.
A Campbell spokesman said the board would name a new chairman closer to Johnson's departure, and one analyst said it was not certain whether Morrison would get that job.

Johnson is a hard-driving Australian known for unchecked enthusiasm while rallying company employees and stockholders and for sharply reviving the earnings of a once-moribund company. He joined Camden, N.J.-based Campbell as its chief executive officer in 1990.

Although Johnson unveiled an ambitious restructuring plan last year aimed at aggressively boosting sales and earnings growth, he had kept close to the vest his own plans following the expiration of his term as chairman.

Morrison said in an interview with Reuters that he will continue the strategic plan adopted last year, which in part aims to plough cost savings from restructuring into increased marketing spending to bolster sales.

Discussing the aims for sales growth, he said, "We've had a wonderful few years on Wall Street. Our market value has tripled since 1990, and now we need to do a better job of winning on Main Street, of winning with consumers."
Analysts said the succession plan and the extension of Johnson's term as chairman will ensure a smooth transition to a new leader with strong marketing abilities.
"This is a good, solid manageable move, and I think that it's a process, not a one-off transaction," said Leonard Teitelbaum, an analyst for Merrill Lynch.
Analysts said Morrison faces a huge challenge filling Johnson's shoes.
After the appointment was announced, the stock slumped. But it rebounded, closing up 62.5 cents at $50 on the New York Stock Exchange.
"I think Campbell shareholders are a little disappointed that David Johnson is leaving so shortly into the new business plan," Prudential Securities analyst John McMillin said.
Added Mitchell Pinheiro, an analyst for Janney Montgomery Scott, "I don't care how dynamic you are, you are going to pale in comparison to David Johnson."
A major challenge Morrison will face is boosting growth in Campbell's core soup brands, which already dominate the U.S. market and are growing abroad, analysts said.
Morrison joined Campbell as president of the Pepperidge Farm division in 1995 after establishing a reputation as a marketing wizard at PepsiCo Inc.'s Frito-Lay unit.
Under his leadership, Pepperidge Farm's annual sales growth rate rose from about 2 percent to nearly 13 percent this year.
Morrison was named president of the international and speciality foods division last November, and his approach is now being carried out across the entire company, Campbell said.
"There is no question in my opinion that this man is very well suited for the task," Teitelbaum said.

Robert Bernstock, the president of Campbell's U.S. grocery division who was also regarded as a contender in what McMillin called a "dogfight" to succeed Johnson, was given the new title of executive vice president in the succession plan.
"They clearly went with a growth-manager (in Morrison)," McMillin said. "He's turned (Pepperidge Farm) Goldfish into a monster. The key now is, will they be able to hold on to Bernstock?" he said.

Another key move in the succession was the elevation to executive vice president of Chief Financial Officer Basil Anderson, a former Scott Paper Co. executive and key engineer of that firm's turnaround under Al Dunlap, Teitelbaum said.
"We're going to need some very strong financial discipline to take this company up to the next notch," he said.
